archetype.name: Rebuilding (bottoming out)
archetype.definition: A team in its second straight last-place season. It is out-chanced at 5-on-5 by the widest margin in the league, and its roster has too little up front to change that this year.

report.headline: Worst team in the league by process and results, and not just unlucky
report.take:
Vancouver sits 32nd of 32 on the site at 6-19-1. That is not a cold start for a decent team. It is the continuation of last year's 25-49-8, 58-point season, which also finished 32nd. The current pace of 41 standings points would be worse still. Only two seasons ago this franchise put up 109 points and won seven playoff games, so the slide has been steep and fast. The record matches the underlying play. The Canucks rank last in Goal Diff / GP at -1.54, last in xGF % at .392 and 30th in CF % at .45. They are not losing coin flips. They are being territorially overrun most nights.

Three things drive the damage. The first is 5-on-5 play, where opponents generate far more chances than Vancouver does. The second is a penalty kill at .612, 31st and sixteen points below the league's .772. That turns every trip to the box into a likely goal. The third is goaltending that has made a bad situation worse: team GSAx is -11.7, last in the league. That last number is mostly one man. Kevin Lankinen has an .815 save % and -14.5 GSAx in eight starts, while Leevi Merilainen sits at .889 with -1.0 GSAx in 16. Merilainen has been close to an average goalie behind a team that gives up a lot. The defense also bleeds production to wingers, who score well above their norms against Vancouver. Wingers take .511 of the points against, well above the league's .43.

The numbers hide a few things. Pts vs Goal Diff is -5.3, worst in the league, so the record is somewhat harsher than even this goal differential implies. Some correction in close games is likely. The 5-on-5 PDO of 98.5 also suggests a bit of bad bounce. Ignore the all-situations finishing block, though. The .152 shooting % and 1.8 shots a game come from only two listed skaters' rows, not the team. The recent 3-2 run over five games looks better, at a -0.4 differential a game. But it sits inside a 3-7 last ten in which they were outscored 42-27, exactly their November line. There is a power play near league average (.22, 15th) and a B- blueline, so the floor isn't zero. The forward group grades D-, though, and its top listed forward has a .297 xGF %.

The direction is clear. This is a lottery team, and the realistic goal for the rest of the year is respectability, not a push. Steadier goaltending from Merilainen and a penalty kill that can't stay this historically bad should lift the points percentage somewhat. Nothing in the shot or chance data suggests a team that will climb out of the Pacific basement.

strengths.title: Power play holds league average
strengths.body: At .22 the power play ranks 15th, a hair under the league's .225. It is the one special-teams or 5-on-5 unit that isn't bottom-tier. Last season's .218 and the years before were in the same range, so this looks like a stable baseline rather than a hot streak.

strengths.title: Blueline is the best group
strengths.body: The defense grades B-, far ahead of the D- forwards and goalies. Elias Pettersson is 12th of 36 on his tab while logging 18.72 minutes a night. His -8 and .383 xGF % show he is swimming against the team's chance deficit, not causing it. This is the part of the roster worth building around.

strengths.title: Merilainen gives a playable floor
strengths.body: In 16 starts Leevi Merilainen has an .889 save % and -1.0 GSAx, essentially average given the volume he faces. The team's -11.7 GSAx is more than accounted for by Lankinen's -14.5. Riding Merilainen should stop some of the bleeding without any change in team play.

concerns.title: Badly out-chanced at 5-on-5
concerns.body: An xGF % of .392 is last in the league, and a CF % of .45 is 30th. Vancouver spends most of its even-strength time defending and generates little. This is not new: last season's xGF % was .442, and it has fallen further. With a D- forward group, this is the structural problem and it will last.

concerns.title: A broken penalty kill
concerns.body: The kill is at .612, 31st and sixteen points below the league average. Even last season's poor .715 was far better. A number this extreme usually drifts back toward the pack, but Lankinen's struggles and a chance-starved team make a full recovery unlikely.

concerns.title: Lankinen's starts are near-automatic losses
concerns.body: An .815 save % and 5.69 GAA across eight starts, with -14.5 GSAx, put him 72nd of 72 on the goalie tab. Unless that changes, every start he makes is a large handicap for a team that already can't afford one.

trend.note: A 2-13 October with a 10-game losing streak gave way to a 3-7 November. November's goals for and against per game barely moved from October's. The recent 3-2 stretch is a small blip inside the same profile.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games: two weak offenses, then elite Boston
weekAhead.body:
The trip opens in Detroit and Philadelphia, two of the league's weakest attacks: offense ranks 30th and 29th. Both have poor power plays, Detroit at .2 and Philadelphia at .181. That matters because Vancouver's kill is its most exploitable hole, and these two are poorly equipped to punish it. Philadelphia already beat Vancouver 3-1 in Vancouver earlier this month. Its .44 xGF % is nearly as poor as Vancouver's, though, so that game should be the closest thing to an even matchup. Detroit is tighter defensively, allowing 24.6 shots a game (5th), and drives possession at a .51 CF %, which plays against Vancouver's biggest weakness.

Boston is a different animal: 15-7-1, third on the site, A goaltending with 11.7 GSAx and a .91 save %. It also allows the fewest points to wingers in the league. Coming at the end of a three-game road swing, that game projects as a clear loss for the league's worst chance-share team. A split of the first two would count as a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Weak power plays blunt the PK problem
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's PP ranks 24th and Philadelphia's 28th, and Boston's sits 26th. Vancouver's .612 kill has turned penalties into goals all season. This week's opponents are among the least likely to cash in, so it is a chance for the kill to steady.

keyMatchups.title: Philadelphia leaks points to centers
keyMatchups.body: The Flyers rank 32nd at holding centers, and their forwards overall rank 29th. With a .44 xGF % and a 29th-ranked offense, they are the most winnable game on the trip if Vancouver's centers can find the open ice.

keyMatchups.title: Boston's goaltending wall
keyMatchups.body: Boston's .91 save % ranks 3rd and its GSAx 4th, and it holds wingers to the fewest points in the league. Vancouver's 24th-ranked offense will struggle to beat that.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal on the trip. Merilainen in all three, or a Lankinen start against Boston, will largely decide whether this is a 0-point or a 3-to-4-point week.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect a modest lift from the current 41-point pace, not a turnaround. Two things should soften: the worst-in-league Pts vs Goal Diff of -5.3, and a penalty kill too extreme to persist. Leaning on Merilainen over Lankinen also removes the worst goaltending outcomes. The xGF % and CF % are both bottom-three and worse than last season's last-place team, and that won't regress, because it is who they are. A finish around 22-27 wins and roughly 50-60 standings points is the realistic band. That is still at or near the bottom of the league.

The goals-against rate should ease toward the high threes rather than stay near 4.4, mostly through goaltending and the kill. Scoring will likely hover in the high twos to around three a game behind a D- forward group and a league-average power play.
swingFactors: Goaltending split between Merilainen and Lankinen
Penalty kill recovering toward league average
Whether close-game luck (Pts vs Goal Diff) evens out

confidence.note: Only 26 games, but the chance and possession data match last season's last-place profile.
